topic: The Elegance of Dandelin Spheres: Proving Conic Sections
target_audience: High school students (Advanced Geometry) and undergraduate math enthusiasts

sections.title: The Slice: From 3D to 2D
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept of a 'conic section' by intersecting a double cone with a plane. Focus on the visual formation of an ellipse and define it by its locus: the set of points where the sum of distances to two foci is constant.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Geometric Chef' slicing a perfectly conical carrot at an angle with a laser; the resulting cross-section is a smooth, purple-edged ellipse.

sections.title: The Magic Spheres Appear
sections.content: Introduce the Dandelin Spheres: two spheres placed inside the cone, one above the plane and one below. Each sphere is 'inscribed' so it is tangent to the cone (along a circle) and tangent to the cutting plane at exactly one point ($F_1$ and $F_2$).
sections.example: Visualize two glowing soap bubbles inflating inside a glass cone until they are snugly trapped by a tilted glass shelf (the plane).

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Ice Cream Cone Lemma
sections.content: Establish the critical geometric tool: tangents from a single point to a sphere are equal in length. This is essential for the transition to the formal proof.
sections.example: An ant standing at a point $P$ outside a sphere measures the distance to the 'horizon' of the sphere; no matter which direction it looks, the distance to the touch-point is identical.

sections.title: The Visual Proof: Linking Segments
sections.content: Pick an arbitrary point $P$ on the ellipse. Draw segments $PF_1$ and $PF_2$. Show that $PF_1$ is equal to the segment along the cone's surface to the upper circle of contact ($PA$), and $PF_2$ is equal to the segment to the lower circle ($PB$).
sections.example: Use color-coded neon lines: $PF_1$ (blue) and $PF_2$ (red) magically 'fold' onto the surface of the cone to form a single straight line segment $AB$ along the slant height.

sections.title: The Constant Sum
sections.content: Demonstrate that the total length $PF_1 + PF_2$ is always equal to the distance $AB$ along the cone's slant height between the two contact circles. Since the circles are fixed, this distance is constant regardless of where $P$ is moved.
sections.example: A 'Space Navigator' notices that as their ship travels the elliptical orbit ($P$), the combined length of the two fuel tethers ($PF_1$ and $PF_2$) remains as rigid as a fixed metal rod.

sections.title: Universal Application: Parabolas and Hyperbolas
sections.content: Briefly extend the logic: explain that by tilting the plane further, we interact with the spheres differently to create parabolas or hyperbolas, proving all conic sections share this spherical harmony.
sections.example: The 'Geometric Chef' tilts the laser slice more steeply; the soap bubbles shift, and the ellipse 'snaps' into an open parabola, like a spotlight hitting a stage floor.
